components.name: Xray-core
components.purpose: Elarni session metrics, dependency security updates, checked private-field access, context cleanup, static-analysis fixes, endpoint-free probe traces and joined XHTTP probe work, and Hysteria authentication context propagation; AmneziaWG 3.1 client engine, WireGuard DNS and peer validation, explicit TLS verification policy and null-certificate rejection, and exact provider balancer selectors; HTTP proxy TLS ALPN compatibility, synchronized XHTTP/mKCP receive shutdown and XHTTP upload byte accounting before buffer ownership transfer; optional logical asset reader and required physical socket binding for the Windows embedded runtime; optional TUN session admission limits for Windows; case-insensitive Windows process names and executable/folder paths for per-app routing; sandbox-compatible macOS socket ownership lookup, Darwin TUN reader cleanup and idle CPU backoff; Windows TCP full-tuple process attribution, joined TUN reader/session shutdown, UDP ownership and error cleanup, and complete Darwin datagram writes; TUIC v5 client integration with pinned sing-quic, required UDP socket ownership and TLS, strict lossless import/share/backup contracts and isolated interoperability/lifecycle traffic regressions; preserve queued responses on normal WebSocket stream completion while retaining abnormal-close errors; per-core DNS and outbound-manager context ownership for parallel embedded mobile probes; XHTTP XMUX steers new streams away from connections busy downloading, with a tagged loopback latency harness; gRPC copies received hunks into pooled buffers instead of pooling protobuf-owned slices, which ratcheted the heap goal during downloads; TUN admission evicts the longest-idle session when full and frees idle DNS flows after 5 s; XHTTP hedges a stalled HTTP/2 handshake after 1 s and closes its XMUX clients when the core stops; stable per-session Windows TUN adapter names, with the adapter parked between connects; QUIC path-MTU discovery on Android for Hysteria and XHTTP/3; gRPC and Hysteria close and forget their pooled clients when the core stops, so a stopped core's connections and the core itself no longer outlive it (Hysteria after XTLS/Xray-core#7107), with pool-release tests; a consumed session ActivityTimer drops its cancel callback, because the stopped runtime timers that still point to it kept the session context and the stopped core reachable for up to the idle timeout, and the gRPC dialer keeps copies of the session ID and outbounds instead of the first dial's context and connection, which gRPC's stopped idle timer kept for up to 30 min; loopback re-entry keeps its origin's SkipDNSResolve instead of forcing it, so the re-entered policy can resolve hostnames for IP rules; WireGuard retries a failed start instead of closing its TUN; XHTTP retires a shared connection only on transport failure or its own setup/response bound, not when a caller gives up, with a test-only setup-timeout override and the request-lifetime tests next to the transport; XHTTP packet-up dials the next XMUX connection's HTTP/2 handshake before moving its posts there and keeps posting on the old one meanwhile (at most 64 requests past its limit), so a request-limit rotation no longer holds uploads for a TCP and TLS handshake, with a loopback rotation test; XHTTP XMUX gives UDP flows other than QUIC their own connection within maxConnections (TCP streams keep the rest), because a download's 4 MB HTTP/2 window queued at the server in front of a call or game on a shared connection delayed it by seconds, with a loopback test on an emulated 20 Mbps, 50 ms line and the line emulator shared with the tagged latency harness; buffered writes flush and continue after a partial buffer write (upstream #6723), which failed Trojan connections whose first payload exceeded the buffer's free space; TUIC sends its CONNECT alone after 100 ms without a first payload, or once the client half-closes without one, so servers that speak first (SMTP, IMAP, MySQL) are reached; WireGuard reads each UDP reply whole instead of truncating it at 8 KiB; XHTTP posts and a session's current upload connection hold their XMUX connection open, so retiring an HTTP/3 connection no longer closes it under posts in flight; XHTTP post bodies can be read again, so HTTP/2 resends the posts a front server's graceful GOAWAY left unprocessed instead of ending the session; HTTP/1.1 packet-up pipelines posts on a pool that reuses its connections, counts a post as written once it is on a connection, reads every response in order so a rejected post fails the session, sends again only the posts a server provably did not read (after Connection: close or a clean close), and closes idle or retired upload connections, including one a post returns after its client closed, instead of leaving them to the garbage collector; XHTTP splitConn.Close reports the reader close error; an embedder can report through internet.SocketPathChanged that its required socket binding moved, and WireGuard then reopens its socket there; the log tap names the level it keeps, so messages neither it nor the handler wants are not built; the WireGuard netstack returns injected packet buffers to gVisor's pools, caches tunnel DNS answers for their TTL, caps TCP receive buffers at 2 MiB (a stalled reader held 4 MiB each), passes queued packets to wireguard-go in batches, and lowers a tunnel MTU above the standard engine's smaller message buffers; the WireGuard bind reads and writes datagram batches with recvmmsg/sendmmsg on Linux, while AmneziaWG keeps single-datagram batches; direct UDP flows on Unix wait for a datagram without a buffer and borrow a pooled 64 KiB one to read it whole (each waiting flow held 64 KiB); the HTTP, TLS, BitTorrent and uTP sniffers reject a short first payload from the bytes they have, so a connection that starts with a few non-matching bytes is routed at once instead of after the 200 ms sniffing deadline; a Hysteria stream past the server's stream limit waits for credit instead of failing, without holding the client lock; TUIC enlarges its UDP socket buffers, which quic-go cannot reach behind the ownership wrapper, and starts with a 16 MiB connection window so two stalled downloads no longer block new streams; XHTTP's HTTP/2 client advertises 2 MiB stream windows instead of Go's 4 MiB, which each stalled download kept full; on Windows the WireGuard netstack's gVisor reads time from the performance counter, because Go's monotonic clock there moves in system-timer steps, so gVisor measured short round trips as zero and its RACK loss detection resent segments in flight; TUN TCP buffers are capped at 1 MiB receive and 2 MiB send (a stalled app or upload held 8 and 6 MiB); the Linux TUN opens with a virtio_net_hdr and TCP segmentation offload so gVisor exchanges 64 KiB segments with the kernel; TUN TCP connections hand gVisor up to 64 KiB per write and, while the stack holds more, take up to eight buffers per read instead of one; the TUN stack starts its packet reader only after its handlers are set; Linux process lookup tries the recent socket owners before scanning every process

components.name: libXray
components.purpose: Elarni FFI integration, bounded runtime metrics and ping controls, dependency security updates, parallel JSON probes with serialized startup/asset loading and joined cleanup quarantine, sanitized stage/status results, disposable DNS controls, exact HTTP response contracts, active packet-path probes, registered probe cancellation, enclosing deadlines, and distinct packet-path DNS failures; strict complete client profile import, 3x-ui protocol and transport preservation, WireGuard/AmneziaWG exports, compatible Clash graphs, and Telegram handoff validation; core DNS bootstrap host matching, TLS/REALITY/ECH/encryption and paired protocol traffic checks, and full-profile FFI routing checks; Windows helper, encrypted catalog, bounded subscriptions and QR import, transactional geodata revisions and independent elevated TUN validation; authenticated Windows listeners, opt-in runtime metrics streaming, bounded memory/session controls and dynamic WFP route enforcement; Incy input normalization using the official crypt1 codec, provider sharing restrictions and local QR encoding; shared pinned subscription downloads, ordered fallback approvals, domain migration, provider banners, verified TLS fronting/ClientHello fragmentation and cancellable desktop fetch operations; password-encrypted portable catalog backups with shared validation; release in-memory geodata after reusable Windows VPN shutdown; TUIC v5 client integration with pinned sing-quic, required UDP socket ownership and TLS, strict lossless import/share/backup contracts and isolated interoperability/lifecycle traffic regressions; stable per-session Windows TUN adapter names; Windows helper install hashes while copying, pre-launches the installed copy and runs from the MSI; the Windows catalog lease process serves loadCatalog/saveCatalog for its owner; a core stop/start regression for gRPC, Hysteria and XHTTP that checks sockets and goroutines return to baseline and the stopped cores become unreachable, and the unelevated staleVPNGuard check that lets Windows connects and app start clear a crashed helper's DNS guard; Windows TUN MTU 9000; the Clash alias walk charges queued nodes against its expansion budget, so self-referencing anchors cannot exhaust memory; the subscription User-Agent carries the app version, which the elarni-core fetch test checks against pubspec.yaml; compiled-routing tests that load the Rust compiler's output into Xray's router, including loopback re-entry; elarni-core --uninstall-helper, which the MSI runs on uninstall to stop running helper copies, clear a stale DNS guard and delete the helper folder; CI names the pinned wintun.dll so its load test cannot skip; the Windows benchmark binding reads the socket family before bind and rejects unknown interface indexes; the TUN DNS outbound forwards query types other than A/AAAA (HTTPS/SVCB excepted) to the profile's first IP resolver through the profile's DNS route instead of answering them empty; the Windows physical binding reports a default route that moved to another interface, so WireGuard leaves the old adapter; Windows TUN routes keep each included prefix instead of merging it into a covering route, so a host listed beside a default still outranks a longer physical route; Clash Hysteria2 up/down and hop-interval follow Mihomo (a bare number is Mbps, B is bytes, decimal prefixes, unparsed rates ignored, N-M hop ranges with a 5 s floor); v2rayN VMess QR codes keep the gRPC authority from host and the insecure, vcn and pcs certificate policy; WireGuard links and configs accept v2rayN's reserved bytes (1,2,3); Clash ws-opts read the Host header in any case, so it becomes the TLS SNI as in Mihomo; base64 feeds whose text starts with a BOM, or that are unpadded and wrapped into lines, import; the app log tap tells the core its level, and geodata reduction decodes one entry at a time instead of the whole list; macOS and Windows run the core on two Ps unless GOMAXPROCS is set, which cut CPU per GB for WireGuard and Hysteria2 on macOS by more than half and halved it in Windows VPN mode

components.name: tun2proxy
components.purpose: bounded dual-stack synthetic DNS allocation, packet-tunnel restoration, role metrics, joined session shutdown, preservation of fragmented DNS-over-TCP responses, and unconnected SOCKS UDP relay sockets compatible with Darwin send_to, and TCP_NODELAY on the proxy connection

components.name: wireguard-go
components.purpose: message buffers sized for one packet (2016 bytes) instead of 64 KiB on desktop and Android, since Xray's bind and gVisor TUN use no UDP GSO/GRO or TUN offload; a test reads its atomic counter for go vet
